rationale:
Same drawing, new rendering. Silhouette, pose, design intent and front-facing cue are untouched — this is a palette and lighting pass only, and that is enforced mechanically rather than promised: the transparent mask is byte-identical to the previous grid, and every outline pixel that touches background is still the #120b10 anchor.

Palette goes from 23 flat colours to 55. The old version gave each material one flat fill plus at most one hard shadow shape. Now every material carries a real ramp, and each ramp shifts hue as it descends instead of running a pure value slide: the light end is warm, the shadow end turns cool and plum. Helmet steel gets 5 steps (#96a5a9 warm grey down to #232c39 cold slate); the coat wool gets 6 (#c8cfbb to #313d44) because it is the biggest mass and needs the most room to turn; skin gets 5 (#f6c795 on the upper-left brow to a plum-cool #5a3430 in the jaw shadow); rust leather 5; nylon rig 4; trouser canvas 4; ivory 4; amber glass 4; boot leather, gunmetal, goggle rubber and injector charge 3 each; plus three inks and two grime tones.

Light is a single upper-left key applied by one consistent rule set. Any pixel whose neighbour above belongs to a different material is an upward-facing plane and takes a light step; the lower-right boundary of every mass takes a dark step; a mass that borders actual background at its top-left takes an extra rim step. That rim is what puts hard edge-lighting on the helmet crown, the brim lip, the shoulder tops and the outer arm. The first two rules together mean every material seam renders as dark-above / light-below, so the coat hem over the trousers, the boot cuffs, the glove cuffs and the collar now read as overlapping layers rather than abutting colour fields.

The old style's hard vertical split at x>=32 survives as a vestige — a soft left-to-right falloff plus a small extra step-down past x32 — so the graphic plane change is still legible without being a slab.

Wear is deterministic, seeded per pixel, and zoned rather than sprayed: chipped paint on the helmet crown, polished highs and dark pits on the glove leather, dust through the coat hem and thighs, heavy grime on the boot toes, scuffs on the gunmetal and the webbing. Blobs only one or two pixels thick are exempt — the goggle strap, the brim and the piping stay clean, because noise on a one-pixel band reads as dithering, not as wear. Interior ink now lifts too: outline against background holds #120b10, but ink inside the form steps up to #1c1421 or #2b2032 where light reaches it, so internal lines stop reading as holes punched through the figure.

What it sacrifices: it is no longer flat-graphic in the strict sense. The original's whole proposition was near-textureless colour blocking, and that purity is gone; this now sits toward the rendered end of the lineup, which is the point of the note but is a genuine loss of the style's distinctiveness. Up close the speckle on the gloves and boots is assertive, and it is only doing real work above roughly 40px. The asymmetry is unchanged, so the pose still will not mirror cleanly for a left-facing frame.
frontFacingCue:
Unchanged in structure; the render pass only strengthened it. (1) The goggle band: a full-width dark housing across the head carrying two amber lenses split by a nose bridge, now with a hot #ffe7a8 glint on the upper-left of each lens and glass that deepens toward its lower edge, so it reads as curved glass rather than a painted shape. It is still the highest-chroma element on the sprite and it is unmistakably a face plane. (2) Below it, four rows of bare skin, now modelled instead of flat: warm #f6c795 across the upper-left brow and cheek falling to plum-cool #5a3430 at the right jaw, with the mouth bar and the neck core held at near-ink #241a2a exactly as in the flat version, so the nose, mouth and chin all turn. The dark maroon hair columns flanking the face keep their own three values and still separate hard from the skin. (3) The chest: a bone cross on a dark front-plane rig, an object that only exists on the front of a torso, with the rig panel now turning from a lit left edge into shadow so the cross sits on a surface rather than a hole.

Head/shoulder clearance is structural and untouched. The chin ends at r19; the neck at r20-r21 is only 6px wide, so real background is visible on both sides of it; the collar at r22 is interior dark; shoulders do not begin until r23. Nothing rises above the shoulder line except the head — the injector's plunger cap still tops out at r25, at the shoulder, far outboard at x0-x7. Verified in grayscale: the head remains the brightest region on the sprite by a clear margin, so the eye still lands on the face first.
smallCheck:
Checked at 28px and 20px tall, nearest-neighbour, composited on a checkerboard so transparency was visible during the check.

At 28px it holds, and holds slightly better than the flat version did. The extra value steps survive downsampling as soft form rather than detail, so the helmet still turns, the brim keeps its lit top and dark underside, and the coat no longer collapses into one uninflected slab. Every load-bearing read is present: pale helmet stripe, amber goggle band, skin jaw, bone cross on the dark rig, two rust mitts, the amber injector column on the left, dark chunky boots. As before, the neck gap closes and the head sits directly on the shoulders, separating by value only — overhanging brim and near-ink collar against bright skin.

At 20px it is honestly getting mushy, the same as the original. The goggle band, helmet stripe, chest cross and injector column still read; everything else reduces to value. The mouth bar, the lens glints, the knuckle divisions and the needle are gone, and the needle thins to a thread that will disappear against a busy background.

The wear speckle does not survive either reduction — it averages out into slightly dirtier material rather than sparkling, which is the intended failure mode. Grayscale at both sizes confirms the hierarchy is intact: head brightest, coat mid, rig and boots at the floor. The rust mitts sit close to the coat in luminance and are separated by hue, which was equally true of the flat version.

Transparency was verified by decoding the emitted PNG back from bytes: colour type 6, exactly two alpha values (0 across 1363 pixels, 255 across 1709), all four corners transparent, and no visible pixel matching the RGB stored under the transparent pixels — so colour-keying cannot punch holes through the sprite.
